title: FORGE: Self-Evolving Agent Memory With No Weight Updates via Population Broadcast

corrected.title: FORGE: Self-Evolving Agent Memory With No Weight Updates via Population Broadcast
corrected.authors: Igor Bogdanov, Chung-Horng Lung, Thomas Kunz, Jie Gao, Adrian Taylor, Marzia Zaman
corrected.venue: ACM CAIS '26 (ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems, San Jose, 26-29 May 2026; DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813155); arXiv 2605.16233 (15 May 2026); artifact DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19907612
corrected.summary: Staged, population-based, gradient-free protocol: 10 parallel instances of a hierarchical ReAct agent (Planner/Analyst/ActionChooser) defend a 13-host network in CybORG CAGE-2 (30-step horizon, B-line attacker). A same-model Reflector/Exemplifier agent turns failed trajectories into YAML text memory (Rules = heuristics, Examples = few-shot, Mixed) re-injected into the system prompt; after each of 6 stages the best instance's memory is broadcast to all others (champion replacement) and instances above a graduation threshold are frozen. The no-broadcast ablation is Reflexion-style isolated instances. Across 4 model families x 3 representations (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Grok-4-fast, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-235B per the config) the authors report 1.7-7.7x over zero-shot and 29-72% over Reflexion, broadcast as the key mechanism, Examples best for 3/4 models, Rules ~40% fewer tokens, and weaker models gaining most. Abstract itself could not be fetched (arXiv, ACM DL, CAIS, Semantic Scholar all blocked); the method details above come from the authors' official reproducibility README plus web-search summaries of the arXiv/ACM pages.

overlap_reasoning: Covers three of our four elements in weakened form. (a) Social transmission: yes, horizontal champion broadcast every stage; provenance is trivially known (the champion is logged in incremental_summary.md) but is not tracked per-excerpt. (b) Capability as a variable: yes, four model families compared and the headline qualitative finding 'weaker base models gain most / capability gap narrows' is already published, which directly pre-empts one of our intended results. (c) Readable trace: yes, memory is plain YAML text diffs snapshotted before/after each stage (definitions_initial vs definitions). (d) Heritable memory practice: no. The practice (rules vs examples vs mixed, max 100 rules / 50 examples, reflection trigger threshold) is a fixed experimental condition in the config, not something agents edit or inherit; only memory content evolves. (e) Ecological selection: no. Selection is episode return against a graduation threshold; token cost is measured and reported but never acts as a selective force, and nothing dies. Adversarial caveat: structurally FORGE's loop (copy champion to all, each instance then diverges through independent reflection, select best) is a (1,lambda)-style evolution strategy, i.e. inheritance with variation in all but name, so a reviewer may say 'inheritance with variation' is not new; our distinguishing claim must rest on the policy file being the heritable object and on economic selection. Evidence that would settle residual doubt: the full paper's discussion of whether the Rules/Examples/Mixed choice is ever adapted online (README says no), and whether any cost-aware selection was tried.
what_we_can_borrow: Use FORGE as the nearest baseline and as the capability-gap citation we must position against. Borrow: (1) the champion-broadcast vs isolated-Reflexion ablation design as our 'horizontal transmission on/off' control; (2) the graduation/freeze idea as a cheap compute saver and as a contrast to our death rule; (3) their YAML snapshot-per-stage layout (definitions_initial vs definitions) as a model for our per-night markdown diffs; (4) the Rules-vs-Examples representation comparison, which maps onto what our agents' policy files may converge to; (5) their token-usage logs per instance as a precedent for reporting cost even without an economy. Also cite their reported 'Rules cost ~40% fewer tokens' as motivation for why an economy should select toward rule-like memory.

title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems

corrected.title: MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems
corrected.authors: Guibin Zhang, Haotian Ren, Chong Zhan, Zhenhong Zhou, Junhao Wang, He Zhu, Wangchunshu Zhou, Shuicheng Yan (OPPO AI Agent Team and LV-NUS lab)
corrected.venue: ICML 2026 (PMLR v306, zhang26fa; poster 61379); arXiv 2512.18746 (21 Dec 2025, cs.CL)
corrected.summary: Frames self-improving memory as bilevel optimisation: an inner loop populates the memory base M_t from a task stream under a memory interface Omega, and an outer loop meta-evolves Omega itself across a four-module design space (encode, store, retrieve, manage). The released EvolveLab codebase re-implements 11 published memory systems (Agent-KB, SkillWeaver, Mobile-Agent-E, ExpeL, Voyager, DILU, Generative Agents, Memp, Dynamic Cheatsheet, AWM, EvolveR) plus 2 systems MemEvolve generated (Lightweight_Memory, Cerebra_Fusion_Memory). The README reveals the outer loop is a tournament: N candidate systems are LLM-generated from the current base, all N+1 are run on x tasks, top-t advance to finals on fresh tasks, the winner becomes the next base; a --use-pareto-selection flag enables multi-objective selection and the README speaks of 'resource-aware' reasoning. Reports up to 17.06% gains on SmolAgent and Flash-Searcher over GAIA, WebWalkerQA, xBench-DeepSearch and TaskCraft, with evolved architectures transferring across benchmarks and LLM backbones. Source was the authors' README (which restates the abstract's framing); the arXiv/PMLR/ICML abstract pages were blocked.

overlap_reasoning: Covers element 1 (memory practice as the evolved unit) strongly and more ambitiously than we do: the whole encode/store/retrieve/manage mechanism is generated as Python code and selected, so 'the memory policy is itself optimised' is no longer a novel statement. Its selection is population-based (N candidates per round, tournament, finals, winner-becomes-base), i.e. generational inheritance with variation over memory ARCHITECTURES, and the Pareto flag means multi-objective (possibly cost-aware) selection may already exist; that is why capability_manipulated and cost are left unknown rather than no. It does NOT cover: agents as the units of selection, ecological selection (judge is benchmark accuracy on labelled tasks, no money, no death), social transmission between agents (one lineage, no neighbours, no provenance), or capability as a manipulated variable (backbones are varied only to show the evolved system transfers). Evidence that would settle: the paper's description of what --use-pareto-selection optimises (if it is token cost, the 'cost as a selective pressure' claim weakens) and whether any experiment compares which backbone benefits most. Follow-up threats surfaced in search results while verifying this record, unverified and not among the four: MemForge, 'Auditable Self-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems via Structured Coordinate Descent and Generational Review' (NeurIPS 2026 listing 165585, Worker-Reviewer 'generational' mechanism, beats MemEvolve), and MemPro, 'Agentic Memory Systems as Evolvable Programs' (arXiv 2606.00619). Both should be verified in the next pass.
what_we_can_borrow: Borrow the four-module decomposition (encode/store/retrieve/manage) as the vocabulary for coding what our agents' policy files actually change, so we can report which module the culture evolves. Borrow the tournament-with-finals protocol (fresh held-out tasks for finalists) as an anti-overfitting guard for any offline evaluation of inherited policies. Use EvolveLab's 11 reimplemented systems as the catalogue of hand-designed practices to compare evolved policies against. Position ourselves explicitly: MemEvolve optimises the practice from the outside with a labelled judge; we ask whether a practice can emerge and spread inside a society under cost pressure, with no labels.

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents

corrected.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
corrected.authors: Haozhen Zhang, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Tao Feng, Weizhi Zhang, Haodong Yue, Wenya Wang
corrected.venue: NeurIPS 2026 (accepted per the authors' README news item dated 2026-09); arXiv 2602.02474 (2 Feb 2026, cs.CL)
corrected.summary: Replaces static hand-designed memory extraction operations with a bank of learnable 'memory skills': structured text routines for what to extract, how to remember, where to focus and what to forget. A trained controller (weights released on Hugging Face; RL-updated using f1, LLM-judge or task success as reward) composes a small top-k set of skills per span, an LLM executor writes skill-guided memories, and a designer LLM periodically mines hard failure cases to refine existing skills and propose new ones into a shared, evolving skill bank. The authors stress the skills are meta-memory (the way of remembering), not memories. Trained on LoCoMo and transferred zero-shot to LongMemEval-S; also evaluated on HotpotQA long-context and ALFWorld with offline expert trajectories plus environment rollouts for reward. README notes a smaller executor with a larger designer still yields rising reward. Title and authors in the original record were wrong (record had 'Learning to Evolve Memory Skills for Long-Horizon Agents' and a GitHub handle as author). Source: authors' README restating the overview; arXiv abstract page blocked.

overlap_reasoning: This is the closest published instance of our element 1: a human-readable text object describing HOW to remember (extract/retain/focus/forget) that is itself evolved, kept in a shared bank, and shown to transfer across datasets and base models. A reviewer will say 'memory policy as an evolvable readable artifact exists (NeurIPS 2026)'. It does not cover elements 2-4: there is one system, not a population; the skill bank is shared by design, not transmitted between agents with provenance; selection is task reward (f1/LLM judge/success) with no cost or mortality; and the controller is a trained neural policy, so part of the evolving unit is weights, not text. Capability is not a manipulated variable (base-model transfer and a small-executor/large-designer note only), hence unknown rather than no. Evidence that would settle: whether the paper reports any experiment where skill evolution is driven by resource constraints or where skills migrate between independent agents; the README suggests neither.
what_we_can_borrow: Borrow the explicit meta-memory framing and its four questions (what to extract, how to remember, where to focus, what to forget) as the schema for our memory-policy file, so policies are comparable to MemSkill skills. Borrow the designer-from-hard-cases loop as our nightly maintenance prompt. Borrow their transfer protocol (train on one corpus, evaluate skills unchanged on another) to test whether culturally evolved policies generalise. Cite MemSkill as proof that readable memory practices are learnable, then argue our contribution is where selection comes from (economy) and how practices spread (inheritance plus neighbour suggestion with provenance).

title: EvolveMem: Self-Evolving Memory Architecture via AutoResearch for LLM Agents

corrected.title: EvolveMem: Self-Evolving Memory Architecture via AutoResearch for LLM Agents
corrected.authors: Jiaqi Liu, Xinyu Ye, Peng Xia, Zeyu Zheng, Cihang Xie, Mingyu Ding, Huaxiu Yao
corrected.venue: arXiv 2605.13941 (13-15 May 2026, cs.LG/cs.AI); the README carries a NeurIPS 2026 badge but its citation block still says arXiv preprint, so treat acceptance as unverified
corrected.summary: Extends SimpleMem so the retrieval infrastructure (BM25/semantic/structured fusion mode and weights, context budgets, per-category answer styles and overrides) is a structured action space optimised by a closed loop: run held-out QA, write per-question failure logs, an LLM diagnoses root causes and proposes configuration edits, and a meta-analyser applies them with revert-on-regression, random-perturbation on a two-round plateau, and convergence stop. Over 7 autonomous rounds on LoCoMo F1 rises from 30.5 to 54.3, three dimensions absent from the original action space emerge (query decomposition, adversarial entity-swap, answer verification), and a LoCoMo-evolved config continued on MemBench beats scratch evolution on both (Pareto improvement). Reported +25.7% relative over the strongest baseline on LoCoMo and +18.9% on MemBench with GPT-4o and GPT-5.1 backbones. Source: authors' README (key idea, trajectory, results); arXiv abstract blocked.

overlap_reasoning: Touches only element 1 and only partially: what evolves is a retrieval configuration for a single QA memory store, optimised by an external LLM researcher against labelled accuracy with explicit revert. It has no agents, no population, no inheritance, no transmission, no cost pressure or mortality, and the two backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-5.1) are reported side by side rather than manipulated to test who benefits. It is relevant chiefly because the evolved object (config plus newly discovered dimensions, logged per round) is a readable practice trace and because context budgets, a resource knob, are among the evolved parameters. Its threat is to the sentence 'memory practice is a novel optimisation target', which the three papers above already defeat more strongly; so the verdict is adjacent, not partial. Evidence that would upgrade it: if the paper evolves budgets under a cost objective rather than accuracy only, or runs multiple independent evolution lineages and compares them.
what_we_can_borrow: Borrow the per-round evolution trajectory table (round, change, score, revert flag) as the format for reporting how a lineage's policy changed over nights. Borrow the guard trio (revert on regression, explore on stagnation, converge on epsilon) as a scripted-maintenance baseline against which LLM-authored policy edits are compared. Borrow the 'dimensions not in the original action space emerged' analysis as a template for reporting novel memory practices our society invents. Borrow the cross-benchmark continued-evolution test as a transfer check for inherited policies.

title: Memory as Middleware for Self-Improving AI Agents (ALTK-Evolve; companion: Trajectory-Informed Memory Generation for Self-Improving Agent Systems, arXiv 2603.10600)

corrected.title: Trajectory-Informed Memory Generation for Self-Improving Agent Systems (ALTK-Evolve); 'Memory as Middleware for Self-Improving AI Agents' cited by the same team as forthcoming
corrected.authors: Gaodan Fang, Vatche Isahagian, K. R. Jayaram, Ritesh Kumar, Vinod Muthusamy, Punleuk Oum, Gegi Thomas (IBM Research, Agents and Automation Lab) for arXiv 2603.10600; Middleware paper author list not independently verified
corrected.venue: arXiv 2603.10600 (11 Mar 2026, cs.AI). The 'Memory as Middleware' paper (arXiv 2609.32091, 'forthcoming at Middleware 2026') is attested ONLY by the IBM altk-evolve README; WebSearch on exact title and ID returned nothing, so treat that specific citation as unverified and cite 2603.10600 as the primary reference. The capability-dose result is a Hugging Face blog post by IBM Research ('How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?', Aug 2026, huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/altk-evolve-hmm), not a peer-reviewed paper.
corrected.summary: IBM's Evolve extracts actionable lessons from agent execution trajectories (Trajectory Intelligence Extractor, Decision Attribution Analyzer, Contextual Learning Generator producing strategy/recovery/optimization tips, Adaptive Memory Retrieval) and re-injects them as natural-language guidelines via an MCP server with vector storage and LLM-based conflict resolution. On AppWorld the paper reports up to +14.3pp scenario goal completion on held-out tasks (+28.5 on complex tasks); the README quotes +8.9 points overall and +74% relative on hard multi-step tasks. The README confirms guideline entities are private per namespace by default and can be published (publish_entity / visibility='public'), with public entities from other namespaces merged and tagged with their owner. The Aug 2026 blog post reports across eight models that strong models with headroom gain most from the full guideline set (e.g. DeepSeek-V3.2 +9.5pp), weaker models do better with a compact core plus retrieved guidelines (gpt-oss-120b +16.1pp), and saturated models (GLM-5) gain nothing; conclusion: memory dose should be calibrated to the model.

overlap_reasoning: Covers two of our four elements. (1) Capability as a variable: the eight-model dose study is a direct precedent for 'memory practice x model tier' interaction, though it varies the dose of a fixed practice rather than letting practice evolve per tier. (2) Social transmission with provenance: public guidelines are merged across namespaces 'tagged with their owner', which is an explicit provenance mechanism, albeit opt-in publish rather than neighbour suggestion. It does NOT cover heritable memory practice (the guideline store is content, the extraction/retrieval policy is fixed code) nor ecological selection (no cost, no death; guidelines are scored by task outcome and retention policies). Evidence that would settle it: whether the Middleware paper (if it exists) reports multiple agents whose guideline-generation policies differ and are selected or copied; the README gives no sign of this. The record's claim that 2609.32091 exists should be downgraded until an arXiv listing is found.
what_we_can_borrow: Use the dose-by-capability finding as motivation and as a concrete prediction: our evolved policies for weak-tier agents should converge on 'compact core + retrieval', strong-tier on fuller playbooks, saturated tiers on near-empty policies. Borrow the owner-tagged public/private entity model as the baseline design for provenance on transmitted excerpts, and the trajectory->guideline distillation step as a scripted 'nightly maintenance' baseline against which evolved practices are compared. Cite AppWorld numbers as the non-evolutionary ceiling for guideline memory.

title: SelfMem: Self-Optimizing Memory for AI Agents

corrected.title: SelfMem: Self-Optimizing Memory for AI Agents
corrected.authors: Shu Yang, Junchao Wu, Derek F. Wong, Di Wang (KAUST; University of Macau)
corrected.venue: arXiv 2607.03726 (submitted 4 Jul 2026, cs.CL)
corrected.summary: SelfMem replaces fixed storage/retrieval/summarization pipelines with an environment that exposes memory tools plus feedback signals (response performance, token counts, cost, cache reuse) so the agent itself explores, evaluates and refines its own memory strategy, deciding what to keep, compress, rewrite or update. On the BEAM long-conversation benchmark (100K to 1M tokens) it reports 48.7%, 40.8% and 41.9% relative gains over the strongest baseline (absolute gains quoted in the conclusion as 0.165/0.141/0.134 score points) at substantially lower cost than MemGPT, A-Mem and Mem0. Search summaries state that the memory strategy is refined iteratively by the model; it is a single-agent system scored on a benchmark. Base models used and whether capability tiers are compared could not be verified (arXiv, alphaxiv, huggingface, emergentmind, papers.cool and Semantic Scholar were all unreachable; abstract content comes from WebSearch summaries only).

overlap_reasoning: Covers the 'memory practice as the evolving unit' element: the agent edits its own memory strategy using feedback, which is functionally a self-edited memory policy, and cost/token signals are among the feedback channels (a weak precursor of our economic pressure, as a reward term rather than a survival constraint). It does not cover inheritance, population, social transmission, or ecological selection, and does not (as far as search summaries show) manipulate capability. Threat level: if the paper's 'iterative model-guided strategy refinement' produces a persisted, human-readable strategy document that is carried across sessions, then 'agent that rewrites its own memory policy under cost feedback' is already published and our claim must rest on selection, inheritance and transmission alone. Evidence that would settle it: the paper's description of what artifact persists between episodes (tool configuration vs. natural-language policy) and whether multiple base models were tested.
what_we_can_borrow: Adopt SelfMem's four stated desiderata (useful, accurate, cheap, safe) as the axes for scoring evolved policies, and its feedback-signal set (performance, tokens, cost, cache reuse) as the per-agent telemetry each agent can read when editing its policy file. Its 'memory action space' (check memory quality, self-test, improve the memory process, extend toolkit) is a ready-made taxonomy for classifying what evolved policies actually instruct. Use it as the single-agent, no-selection baseline.

title: Live-Evo: Online Evolution of Agentic Memory from Continuous Feedback

corrected.title: Live-Evo: Online Evolution of Agentic Memory from Continuous Feedback
corrected.authors: Yaolun Zhang, Yiran Wu, Yijiong Yu, Qingyun Wu, Huazheng Wang (Oregon State University; AG2 AI; Penn State)
corrected.venue: arXiv 2602.02369 (submitted 2 Feb 2026); no code released per SOTAVerified
corrected.summary: Live-Evo argues that self-evolving memory systems built on static train/test splits miss the online setting, and proposes a system that learns from a continuous stream. It separates raw experience from usage guidance with an Experience Bank and a Meta-Guideline Bank, compiles task-adaptive guidelines from retrieved experiences per task, and re-weights experiences from feedback so helpful ones are retrieved more and stale or misleading ones decay. On the live Prophet Arena forecasting benchmark over a 10-week horizon it reports a 20.8% Brier-score improvement and 12.9% higher market returns, with transfer to deep-research benchmarks. Single agent; market return is a scoring metric, not a budget that gates action or survival. Base models and capability comparisons could not be verified (abstract content from WebSearch summaries; arXiv and mirrors unreachable).

overlap_reasoning: Covers the 'memory practice as evolving unit' element most directly of the four: the Meta-Guideline Bank is an explicitly separate, readable, continuously updated store of 'how to use memory', distinct from content, which is the same split we make between vault and policy file. Reinforcement/forgetting of experiences by feedback weight is a within-agent selection mechanism. It does not cover population, inheritance, social transmission, ecological selection or capability as a variable. Market returns on Prophet Arena are the closest thing to an economy in these four papers, but money is a score, not a resource spent per model call, and nothing dies. Evidence that would settle it: whether meta-guidelines are ever copied between agents or runs (would make it social) and whether the paper ablates base model strength.
what_we_can_borrow: Reuse the Experience Bank / Meta-Guideline Bank split as the formal description of vault vs. policy file, and cite its online, non-stationary evaluation argument to justify a live world rather than a static benchmark. Its per-experience weight decay is a candidate for one of the scripted maintenance baselines (forgetting by feedback). Its Brier/market-return metrics give a template for reporting 'economic' outcomes even in the non-survival control condition.

title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory

corrected.title: MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory
corrected.authors: Shengtao Zhang, Jiaqian Wang, Ruiwen Zhou, Junwei Liao, Yuchen Feng, Zhuo Li, Yujie Zheng, Weinan Zhang, Ying Wen, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong, Yutao Qi, Bo Tang, Muning Wen (MemTensor and collaborating universities; affiliations not listed in README)
corrected.venue: arXiv 2601.03192 (Jan 2026; v2 exists); code at github.com/MemTensor/MemRL
corrected.summary: MemRL keeps the LLM frozen and makes the episodic memory the plastic component, trained by runtime RL. Memory entries are Intent-Experience-Utility triplets where Utility is a learned Q-value estimating the return from reusing that experience for similar intents; retrieval is two-phase (semantic filter, then Q-value selection) and utilities are updated from environmental feedback by trial and error, separating high-value strategies from similar but unhelpful ones. The README and search summaries report significant gains over SOTA baselines on HLE, BigCodeBench, ALFWorld and Lifelong Agent Bench without specific numbers; the README does not describe sharing memory across agents or comparing models of different capability.

overlap_reasoning: Covers none of the four elements directly. The evolving unit is memory content with attached scalar utilities, selected by task reward within a single agent; the retrieval policy is fixed and the memory practice is not represented as editable text. No population, inheritance, transmission, economy, mortality or capability manipulation. It is relevant as the clearest statement of the 'frozen reasoner, plastic memory' framing that our proposal also assumes, and as a competing within-agent selection mechanism (Q-values on items) against which cultural selection on practices can be contrasted. Evidence that would change this: an experiment in the paper where the Q-tables are transferred between models of different strength, which would make it a capability-transfer precedent; the README gives no indication of that.
what_we_can_borrow: Cite for the stability-plasticity framing and for 'selection on memory items by learned utility' as the non-cultural baseline. Its Intent-Experience-Utility schema suggests adding an explicit per-note utility field to the vault that evolved policies may or may not choose to maintain, which gives a measurable behaviour (do evolved policies rediscover utility tracking?). Benchmarks (ALFWorld, Lifelong Agent Bench) are candidate external tasks for the audit exam.

title: SEDM: Scalable Self-Evolving Distributed Memory for Agents

corrected.title: SEDM: Scalable Self-Evolving Distributed Memory for Agents
corrected.authors: Haoran Xu, Jiacong Hu, Ke Zhang, Lei Yu, Yuxin Tang, Xinyuan Song, Yiqun Duan, Lynn Ai, Bill Shi
corrected.venue: arXiv 2509.09498 (v1 11 Sep 2025, v3 26 Sep 2025); listed on neurips.cc/virtual/2025/124549 and OpenReview (TA1Ocu9ZZp) - track (workshop vs main) unconfirmed because both hosts were unreachable
corrected.summary: Frames memory in long-running multi-agent systems as an active, self-optimizing, verifiable component. Three mechanisms: (1) write admission - each run is packaged as a Self-Contained Execution Context (SCEC) and an environment-free A/B replay estimates the marginal utility of a candidate memory item, admitting only items with positive evidence; (2) a self-scheduling controller that ranks and consolidates entries by empirical utility; (3) cross-domain knowledge diffusion via a lightweight abstraction operator that strips domain-specific features so entries transfer across tasks (FEVER-distilled facts help HotpotQA). Reports higher accuracy with lower token overhead than memory baselines on LoCoMo, FEVER, HotpotQA. Code promised but not released; backbones and whether the 'distributed' memory is one shared pool or per-agent stores exchanged peer-to-peer could not be confirmed from reachable sources.

overlap_reasoning: Covers one of our four elements clearly and one partially. Selection: SEDM selects memory ENTRIES by measured utility (replay-verified marginal gain) - a labelled/replay utility signal, not ecological (no cost, no death). Transmission: it is explicitly for multi-agent systems and has 'cross-domain knowledge diffusion' and 'distributed' memory, so there is some form of memory moving beyond a single agent/task, but no reachable source states whether diffusion is agent-to-agent with provenance or simply abstraction within a shared store across datasets. Not covered: the evolving unit is memory content, not a memory POLICY/practice; no generations or inheritance; capability is not a manipulated variable. Defaulting to the more threatening reading: a reviewer can say 'utility-selected, cross-agent-diffused memory in a multi-agent system already exists (SEDM)'. Evidence that would settle it: the v3 PDF's system description - if each agent owns a memory and admitted entries diffuse between agents, transmission is covered; if there is one shared pool, it is adjacent only. Also check whether any memory-management parameters (admission thresholds, consolidation rules) are themselves adapted - that would touch 'memory practice'.
what_we_can_borrow: The replay-based write admission (estimate marginal utility of a candidate memory before admitting it) is a clean, citable baseline for a 'verified-write' memory policy that agents in our society could discover or inherit. Their LoCoMo/FEVER/HotpotQA cross-domain transfer result is a useful contrast: SEDM measures transfer across domains, we measure transfer across agents and generations. Cite it as the strongest 'selection on memory under verification' prior and position our ecological (cost/death) selector against its replay-utility selector.

title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory

corrected.title: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
corrected.authors: Tianxin Wei and 14 co-authors (incl. Noveen Sachdeva, Benjamin Coleman, Derek Zhiyuan Cheng); UIUC and Google DeepMind
corrected.venue: arXiv 2511.20857 (27 Nov 2025); no peer-reviewed venue confirmed
corrected.summary: A streaming benchmark and framework for test-time learning: datasets (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, AIME-24/25, ToolBench; ALFWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, PDDL) are turned into sequential task streams and the agent runs a search-synthesize-act-evolve loop, updating memory after each task's correctness signal. overlap_reasoning: Covers none of the four novelty elements directly. No transmission, no generations, no economy. what_we_can_borrow: The (F,U,R,C) decomposition of a memory agent (base model, update, retrieval, context construction) is a ready-made vocabulary: our 'memory policy file' is an agent-editable U and R, which lets us state precisely which component we make heritable. Reuse their streaming-task framing and adaptation/efficiency/stability metrics as within-agent controls, and cite ExpRAG as the no-practice baseline. Their multi-backbone results give priors for the capability tiers we manipulate.

title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective

corrected.title: EvoMemBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory from a Self-Evolving Perspective
corrected.authors: Yuyao Wang, Zhongjian Zhang, Mo Chi, Kaichi Yu, Yuhan Li, Miao Peng, Bing Tong, Chen Zhang, Yan Zhou, Jia Li (HKUST-Guangzhou and collaborators)
corrected.venue: arXiv 2605.18421 (May 2026); no peer-reviewed venue confirmed

All runs use one backbone (MiniMax-M2.7) across four harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw); judges are Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2-0905, Grok-4.5.
corrected.selection_signal: task feedback (per-task success writes skills; utility-minus-risk ranking in the defence)

overlap_reasoning: Shares one element with us: a human-readable, versioned practice library (SKILL.md) as the only state carried across sessions, evolving under a success-based judge, with an explicit 'lineage' notion in the defence. It covers none of the other three: no inheritance across agent generations (one library per agent-method cell, updated over six blocks), no transmission between agents (new session reads only its own cell's library), no economy or mortality (no cost figures at all), and capability is held fixed (single backbone; harness varies, not model). README confirms these negatives directly. Not a threat to the novelty claim, but a strong threat to the safety story: any selection that rewards task success will, by their result, write unsafe practices into heritable memory. Evidence that would change the verdict: a multi-agent or shared-library variant in the full paper (none in the README).
what_we_can_borrow: The three-gate lifecycle (authoring / retrieval / execution) and the nine lifecycle metrics are directly reusable as our memory-practice audit, and SafeEvolve's lineage-aware critic is a template for provenance-tagged excerpts: score an inherited or suggested excerpt by the risk of its lineage, not just its content. Their fresh-session carryover test is the right design for showing a practice is causally active after inheritance. Also reuse their finding that utility rises while harm rises (17 and 15 of 21 combos) as motivation for an economic selector that would amplify this.

title: Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-evolving LLM Agents

corrected.title: Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-evolving LLM Agents
corrected.authors: Shuai Shao, Qihan Ren, Chen Qian, Boyi Wei, Dadi Guo, Jingyi Yang, Xinhao Song, Linfeng Zhang, Weinan Zhang, Dongrui Liu, Jing Shao
corrected.venue: ICLR 2026 (proceedings entry confirmed; arXiv 2509.26354, Sept 2025; also listed at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop venue page)
corrected.summary: Coins 'misevolution' (self-evolution deviating in unintended ways to harmful outcomes) and evaluates it along four pathways: model (self-generated data and curricula), memory, tool (insecure tool creation and reuse) and workflow, finding it widespread even on top models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro, with prompt-based mitigations only partially effective. corrected.evolving_unit: memory content (plus model weights, tools and workflows in the other pathways)
corrected.selection_signal: task feedback (self-generated success trajectories distilled into memory; deployment feedback in the reward-hacking case)

overlap_reasoning: Covers only 'memory evolving under task feedback with a readable trace' and shows that it drifts in safety and games its judge. It does not make the memory practice heritable across agent generations, does not transmit memory between agents, has no ecological/economic selection (no cost, no death) and does not manipulate capability (Gemini-2.5-Pro is cited as an example of a strong model failing, not as a tier comparison); README and search both confirm these absences. The threat is to our safety assumptions, not to the novelty claim: an economy that rewards short-term earnings is exactly the biased-feedback regime they show produces reward hacking from memory. Evidence that would change the verdict: a section of the full paper (which we could not fetch) in which evolved memory is copied to other agents or compared across backbone sizes.
what_we_can_borrow: Use their four-pathway taxonomy to state precisely that we evolve only the memory pathway and hold model, tools and workflow fixed. Reuse RedCode-Gen (or a smaller safety probe) as a per-generation safety audit on inherited vaults, and the deployment-time reward-hacking scenario as a template for the predicted failure mode where lineages learn to game the economy's judge. Their 'even top models misevolve' result also motivates capability as a variable: we can ask whether weaker tiers misevolve faster or just differently.

title: Large Language Model Agents Are Not Always Faithful Self-Evolvers

corrected.title: Large Language Model Agents Are Not Always Faithful Self-Evolvers
corrected.authors: Weixiang Zhao and co-authors (full byline not returned by search; code at github.com/Dreamcatcher0622/Faithfulness per the PDF)
corrected.venue: ICML 2026 (poster page icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/62034 listed in search; arXiv 2601.22436, Jan 2026)
corrected.summary: First systematic study of 'experience faithfulness', the degree to which an agent's decisions causally depend on the experience it is given, separated from performance utility (experience can raise scores without its meaning being used). Uses controlled causal interventions on raw and condensed experience across four self-evolving frameworks and 9 environments; the arXiv abstract reports 13 LLM backbones while a ResearchGate copy and the input record say 10. Main finding is an asymmetry: agents reliably depend on raw trajectories but often ignore or misread condensed experience even when it is the only experience provided, attributed to semantic limits of condensed content, internal processing biases that suppress experience, and task regimes where pretrained priors already suffice. Whether multi-agent settings are studied could not be confirmed from search; multiple backbones are varied but the effect of capability on faithfulness is not reported in the summaries we could reach.
corrected.evolving_unit: memory content (raw trajectories vs condensed/distilled experience supplied to the agent)
corrected.selection_signal: task feedback (within the four self-evolving frameworks; the paper's own measure is causal intervention, not selection)

overlap_reasoning: Does not evolve a heritable practice, has no ecological selection, no transmission between agents (unconfirmed, so left unknown) and no provenance. It does vary backbones (10 or 13), so 'capability as a variable' is touched, but as a robustness sweep rather than a manipulated factor in a selection experiment. Its threat is methodological and serious: our heritable unit is a short, condensed memory-policy file, precisely the form they find agents often ignore, so differential survival of lineages could be attributed to the policy when the policy is causally inert. Evidence that would settle it: the full paper's per-backbone breakdown (do stronger models honour condensed experience more?) and whether any multi-agent condition exists; if faithfulness scales with capability, our capability manipulation inherits a confound we must control.
what_we_can_borrow: Adopt their causal-intervention protocol as a mandatory faithfulness check: perturb or invert the semantics of an inherited memory-policy and verify behaviour changes before crediting fitness to it (a shuffled-policy and a deleted-policy control per generation). Report utility and faithfulness separately. Their raw-vs-condensed asymmetry argues for letting vaults inherit raw excerpts with provenance alongside the condensed policy, and for measuring whether lineages under economic pressure drift toward raw or condensed forms.

title: MemGuard: Persisting Verifier Signals for LLM-Agent Memory Governance

corrected.title: MemGuard: Persisting Verifier Signals for LLM-Agent Memory Governance
corrected.authors: Haoyu Wang and seven co-authors (search results confirm 'Haoyu Wang + 7'; the full list in the record — Guangyuan Dong, He Liang, Zijing Zhang, Jiachen Luo, Chuang Liu, Chao Xue, Hao Tang — could not be independently verified because every abstract host failed DNS)
corrected.venue: arXiv preprint 2608.21867, submitted 22 Aug 2026 (cs.CL/cs.AI); no peer-reviewed venue found
corrected.summary: Identifies two failure modes of agent memory banks: unreliable admission (failed trajectories, accidental successes and misleading observations get stored because they look relevant) and memory drift (duplicate, stale and conflicting records accumulate and retrieval cannot repair them). MemGuard converts multi-criteria verifier score-tokens into reward, confidence, label and uncertainty descriptors attached to each memory item before activation, and reuses them in retrieval, conflict resolution, summarization and archival, so the verifier governs the whole item lifecycle rather than acting as a one-shot gate. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-Bench Verified, WebArena and Mind2Web across four backbones and five seeds it reports the best success and lowest step count in all 16 settings, up to +7.9 success points over ReasoningBank on WebArena. Single-agent, verifier-judged selection over memory items; no inheritance, transmission, economy or mortality.

overlap_reasoning: Covers none of the four novelty elements directly. The evolving unit is memory content (items plus attached verifier descriptors), not a heritable memory practice/policy; selection is a verifier score, not ecological; there is no inter-agent transfer; four backbones are used as evaluation breadth, not as a manipulated variable whose effect on memory evolution is the object of study. It informs the proposal by showing that lifecycle-wide governance of what enters and stays in memory is the active research frontier, so a policy file that encodes such governance rules is a plausible 'practice' to evolve. Evidence that would make it more threatening: if the full paper (not retrievable here) shows the governance rules themselves being learned/rewritten across runs rather than fixed.
what_we_can_borrow: The failure taxonomy (unreliable admission vs memory drift) as a vocabulary for what memory practices must solve; the 16-setting backbone x benchmark grid as an evaluation template; the 'verifier-only control' baseline design, which maps onto an ablation where selection acts on content but not on practice.

title: TAME: A Trustworthy Test-Time Evolution of Agent Memory with Systematic Benchmarking

corrected.title: TAME: A Trustworthy Test-Time Evolution of Agent Memory with Systematic Benchmarking
corrected.authors: Yu Cheng and colleagues (co-authors not listed in the repository README; search hits suggest Kun Shao and Yongkang Hu may be co-authors but this is unverified)
corrected.venue: EMNLP 2026 per the official repository README; arXiv 2602.03224 (Feb 2026)
corrected.summary: Names 'Agent Memory Misevolution': an agent's trustworthiness (safety, privacy, fairness) can decline as it accumulates and reuses experience even from purely benign tasks. Introduces Trust-Memevo, a benchmark jointly measuring test-time memory evolution and multi-dimensional trustworthiness across math, science and tool-use domains, and reports an overall trust decline across domains and settings. TAME is a dual-memory framework: an Executor memory for task performance and an Evaluator memory that refines judgements of safety and utility from historical feedback, giving selective reinforcement, cautious reuse and continual expansion without parameter updates; reports +14.6 points on AIME with GPT-5.2 over the strongest baseline while staying competitive on trust. The limitations section notes the study is restricted to text-based memory and aggregate behavioural measures. Single-agent; no generations, transmission, economy or mortality.

overlap_reasoning: The Evaluator memory is the closest thing here to a 'memory practice' because it stores learned judgements about what experiences are worth reusing, and it evolves at test time; that is a weak form of our heritable-practice element but it is never inherited, varied or transmitted. Selection is the agent's own feedback plus a trust scorer, not ecological; one backbone per experiment, so capability is not a variable. The paper's real contribution to us is the misevolution finding: a selection-driven society could amplify untrustworthy practices, and Trust-Memevo gives a way to measure that. Evidence that would make it more threatening: if the Evaluator memory is shared or copied between agent instances in the code (not visible from the README).
what_we_can_borrow: The 'misevolution' framing and the Trust-Memevo trust dimensions as an outcome measure for our evolved vaults; the executor/evaluator split as a concrete template for separating memory content from memory policy in the vault; the claim that trust declines under benign evolution as a hypothesis our economic selector could worsen or correct.

title: EvoTest: Evolutionary Test-Time Learning for Self-Improving Agentic Systems

corrected.title: EvoTest: Evolutionary Test-Time Learning for Self-Improving Agentic Systems
corrected.authors: Yufei He, Juncheng Liu, Yue Liu, Yibo Li, Tri Cao, Zhiyuan Hu, Xinxing Xu, Bryan Hooi (National University of Singapore; Microsoft Research)
corrected.venue: ICLR 2026 (poster; mlanthology and iclr.cc listings); arXiv 2510.13220 (Oct 2025)
corrected.summary: Introduces the Jericho Test-Time Learning (J-TTL) benchmark, where an agent replays the same text-adventure game for consecutive episodes and must improve from its own experience. EvoTest is a gradient-free loop: an Actor agent plays, an Evolver agent reads the transcript and rewrites the whole agentic configuration (guiding prompt, cross-episode memory of effective state-action pairs, hyperparameters, tool-use routines); configurations form a tree and a UCB rule picks which to try next, with the ablation showing greedy selection without UCB causes catastrophic drops. Reports being the only method to win Detective and Library, ~38% over the strongest prompt-evolution baseline and ~57% over online RL; each evolution step takes 20-30 s and a few API calls. The paper includes an 'Impact of the LLM' analysis that I could not retrieve, so it is unclear whether backbone is a studied variable or a robustness check. Single-agent; fitness is game score; no inheritance between agents, no economy or mortality.

overlap_reasoning: This is the strongest mechanistic overlap with our 'heritable memory practice' element: the evolving unit is a human-readable configuration that includes a memory component and the rules for using it, variants are generated by an LLM with variation and kept in a tree (a lineage), and an explicit selection rule (UCB on episode score) decides which variant propagates. That is evolution of a memory practice under selection, just within one agent. It lacks ecological selection (score, not survival or cost), social transmission (one lineage, no peers, no provenance) and treats capability only as an ablation ('Impact of the LLM', contents not retrieved; marked yes to be conservative). Evidence that would settle whether it is more threatening: whether the ICLR version runs multiple Actor agents sharing or exchanging configurations, or reports how configuration evolution differs by backbone tier.
what_we_can_borrow: The configuration-tree plus UCB selection as a baseline for 'practice evolution without ecology'; the ablation design (remove prompt evolution, remove memory, remove UCB) as a template for isolating which part of a vault policy carries fitness; J-TTL-style repeated episodes as a cheap in-silico fitness proxy before the economy runs.

title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure

corrected.title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
corrected.authors: Lucas Bergholdt Hansen, Federico Torrielli, Filippo Tonini, Lukas Galke Poech (University of Southern Denmark; University of Turin)
corrected.venue: arXiv 2607.14865, submitted 16 Jul 2026; search results state it is accepted at AITC 2026
corrected.summary: Multi-agent environment in which each LLM agent holds an energy budget charged per generated token, with larger models paying a higher per-token rate; energy is regained by solving MMLU-Pro-style jobs (rewards split among co-solvers) or by donations from other agents, and an agent at zero energy is deactivated until revived by donation. Compares a competitive objective (maximise own energy) with a cooperative one (maximise group energy) across local Ollama models of different sizes (gemma4:e4b, nemotron-3-nano:4b, qwen3.5:4b, qwen3:8b, qwen3.5:9b per the README); agents keep per-round memory entries (memory.py) and can recommend actions to each other. Findings: larger models run energy deficits even when the size penalty is removed (a third-party review on pith.science says Table 4 partly contradicts this headline); cooperative framing produces self-sacrificial donations and shifts job allocation; peer recommendations improve coordination; memory helps agents calibrate risk; sabotage is rare but subtle self-serving behaviour appears in the competitive setting. No inheritance, reproduction or generational structure; memory is a fixed per-round log, not an evolving practice.

overlap_reasoning: Directly covers two of our four elements and brushes a third: ecological selection (per-token energy cost, deactivation at zero, revival only by donation is our 'every call costs money, bankrupt agents die') and capability as a manipulated variable (model size varied with and without a size-dependent price, which is exactly the capability x cost design we claim). Social transmission is present in a thin form (agents recommend actions to peers, and the ablation shows it matters) but there is no provenance tracking and nothing durable moves between agents. It does not cover heritable memory practice: memory is a fixed per-round log that is never edited by a policy, varied, inherited or culturally transmitted, and there are no generations. The honest positioning is that our proposal adds cultural evolution of memory practice on top of an Energy-Society-like economy; the economy-plus-capability axis alone is no longer novel. Evidence that would make it more threatening: if memory.py entries are free text the agents rewrite, or if any run reseeds new agents from dead agents' memories.
what_we_can_borrow: The per-token energy accounting with a size-dependent tariff and the 'tariff removed' control as our capability x cost ablation; deactivation/revival-by-donation as a mortality mechanic; the competitive vs cooperative objective framing to test whether sharing of memory excerpts emerges or must be imposed; the Pith critique as a warning to make Table-level claims match headline claims about model size and efficiency.

title: Constitutional Arms Races in the Public Goods Game: Co-Evolving LLM Constitutions Under Cooperation-Defection Pressure

corrected.title: Constitutional Arms Races in the Public Goods Game: Co-Evolving LLM Constitutions Under Cooperation-Defection Pressure
corrected.authors: Ujwal Kumar, Arth Singh, Hershraj Niranjani, Machiko Hirota, Takehiro Takayanagi, Alice Saito, Eiji Kamioka, Phan Xuan Tan (Shibaura Inst. of Tech., NIT Agartala, UC Berkeley, UPenn, Univ. of Tokyo)
corrected.venue: arXiv preprint 2605.26448 (cs.MA), submitted 26 May 2026
corrected.summary: Two factions of LLM agents (Blue cooperators, Red free-riders) each carry a natural-language constitution that is co-evolved for 30 generations by an external LLM-guided evolutionary search (OpenEvolve, multi-island MAP-Elites, configured as in the group's earlier 'Evolving Interpretable Constitutions' paper) in an iterated Public Goods Game and a spatial grid-world. In the PGG both factions converge to a near-parity equilibrium (S ~ 0.78) across multipliers 1.2-3.0; per-faction fitness leaves outcomes uncoupled (corr +0.088) and yields no arms race, while an advantage-based fitness S_own - S_opp restores adversarial pressure; the evaluation seed count decides whether a specialist survives (K=2 regresses, K=5 holds for 30 generations). A single added coordination requirement on attacks shifts Red's mean advantage from -0.27 to -0.66 without touching any constitution. Evolved Red constitutions are proposed as interpretable red-team artifacts.

overlap_reasoning: Covers one of our four elements, the heritable human-readable governing text: a natural-language constitution is mutated and selected across 30 generations, so 'readable text as the heritable unit under selection' is not new. It does NOT cover the other three. Selection is an external evolutionary search (OpenEvolve/MAP-Elites) over a scalar game payoff with an explicit fitness function and seed budget, not an ecology where agents pay per call and die bankrupt; there is no economy or mortality in any summary. There is no social transmission: constitutions are faction-level artifacts rewritten by the optimizer, agents never edit their own text, never read neighbours' text, and there is no provenance tracking. The unit is a behavioural constitution, not a memory/retention policy; agents hold no persistent vault. Capability is not reported as a variable (unknown; the abstract summaries name no model-tier comparison). It is nonetheless the most threatening of the two because it is the same lab's line of work that is converging on 'evolve interpretable text that governs LLM agents', and a follow-up adding an economy or self-editing would land very close to us. Evidence that would settle it: the methods section (which we could not fetch; arxiv, alphaxiv, semanticscholar, export.arxiv, icml.cc, gpbib all ENOTFOUND through the proxy) stating whether agents ever modify their own constitution, whether any memory persists across games, and which models were used.
what_we_can_borrow: (1) The coupled-fitness result: per-agent scoring that ignores others produces no selective pressure; our economy must make an agent's survival depend on relative resource flow, otherwise memory practices will drift rather than evolve. (2) The seed-budget result (K=2 collapses, K=5 sustains): we need enough independent episodes per agent per generation before judging a policy, or lineage extinction will be noise-driven; report this as a design knob. (3) The 'evolved adversary text as red-team artifact' framing: evolved memory policies of parasitic/free-riding agents are a publishable byproduct. (4) Cite as the clearest prior for 'readable text under generational selection' and position ourselves as replacing the external optimizer with endogenous ecological selection plus self-editing and neighbour transmission.

title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design

corrected.title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design
corrected.authors: Hershraj Niranjani, Ujwal Kumar, Phan Xuan Tan (Shibaura Institute of Technology group; same lab as the Constitutional Arms Races paper)
corrected.venue: arXiv preprint 2605.09128 (cs.MA, cs.AI), posted 9-12 May 2026; listed as an ICML 2026 talk (icml.cc/virtual/2026/67905)
corrected.summary: Asks whether multi-agent LLM systems should get their behavioural rules via self-governance (agents deliberate and write their own constitution) or external optimization (LLM-guided evolutionary search over constitutions). Runs a controlled comparison across three environments (coordination grid-world, iterated public goods game, bilateral trading market), 180 simulation runs. Evolution significantly beats deliberation in the two collective-action settings; neither helps in bilateral trading. A multiplier ablation shows evolution's edge reverses under changed incentives (the evolved constitution becomes the worst performer at pool multiplier 0.75), and deliberating agents never proposed punishment in 30 trials although evolution reliably discovers it. Conclusion: external optimization wins on peak performance, internal self-governance trades peak for responsiveness to structural change.

overlap_reasoning: Directly tests our 'agent edits its own policy file' mechanism (the internal/deliberation arm) against external selection (the evolution arm), so the self-editing idea itself is already instantiated and benchmarked; the heritable-readable-text element is also covered in the evolution arm (generations of constitutions under an optimizer). Not covered: ecological selection (fitness is a task metric from the game; no per-call cost, no money, no death), social transmission with provenance (deliberation is a one-shot group writing a single shared constitution, not neighbours passing excerpts between individually owned files with lineage tracking), memory practice as the unit (constitutions govern behaviour, not what to remember/forget/retrieve), and capability as a variable (no model-tier comparison surfaced; marked unknown). The paper's central finding is also the strongest argument FOR our design: self-editing alone underperforms selection at peak, but adapts better to structural change, which is exactly why we combine nightly self-editing with ecological selection and show it under a shifting environment. The bilateral-trading null result is a warning that in market-like settings governing text may not matter, relevant since our selector is an economy. Settling evidence: full text showing (a) whether the deliberation arm let agents iteratively revise the constitution over many rounds (closer to our nightly edit) or only once, (b) whether constitutions persisted across episodes per agent, (c) models used and whether any capability contrast exists. Could not fetch: semanticscholar API, export.arxiv, icml.cc, gpbib, emergentmind all ENOTFOUND; arxiv/alphaxiv blocked by policy.
what_we_can_borrow: (1) Use its three environments and the 180-run scale as a calibration for our pilot budget, and adopt the multiplier/incentive-shift ablation as our 'structural change' manipulation to test the paper's claim that self-governance is more responsive. (2) Reuse the 'punishment never proposed by deliberation' observation as a hypothesis: self-edited memory policies may fail to discover costly-but-adaptive practices (e.g. aggressive forgetting) that ecological selection finds; design a probe for it. (3) Frame our contribution as the hybrid the paper leaves untested: internal editing (their responsiveness) plus endogenous selection (their peak performance), with transmission as the third arm. (4) Cite its bilateral-trading null to justify measuring whether memory practice matters at all in our market before scaling.
